word:lxx:L700007.explanation: Abadia is a personal name, also rendered Avathia. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:9. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine what is said about the person there. Its normal function is therefore as a proper name preserved in the biblical record.

word:lxx:L700142.explanation: “Angia” is a personal name, also rendered “Anggia,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:15. Because it functions as a proper name and no verse text is supplied here, its significance cannot be explained beyond identifying the person named in that genealogy. The spelling may appear slightly different in English, but the lexical identity remains the same.

word:lxx:L700384.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “gather round”: to bring people together or assemble them in one place. It describes the act of collecting a group, whether people are called together or brought together by circumstances. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, showing a repeated sense of assembling rather than merely being present. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is gathered and why.

word:lxx:L700403.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Aidan; Ethan.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 23:9. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: distinguishing the individual who bears the name. The exact person and significance of the name in that passage require the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L700458.explanation: This adjective means “praiseworthy”: worthy to be admired, honored, or spoken of with approval. It describes a person, thing, or quality that deserves praise rather than blame. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times across ten verses, including passages concerning God’s greatness and human excellence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the person or thing it describes, but its central idea remains deserving commendation.

word:lxx:L700612.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to a “governor of the citadel” or a “guardian”—someone responsible for protecting and overseeing a fortified place. The word can therefore describe a person who holds authority over a citadel while also carrying the duty of guarding it. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 3:13. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a citadel’s appointed protector or governor.

word:lxx:L700689.explanation: “One another” refers to people or things considered mutually or reciprocally, connecting one member with the others in a group. It is a pronoun, so it points back to persons or things already understood from the surrounding sentence rather than naming them. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 40 times, showing a repeated way of expressing mutual relationships or actions. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding words and context.

word:lxx:L700731.explanation: Alsōrēch, also rendered Alsorikh, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as an identifying name in the Greek LXX text and appears only once in that corpus, at Judges 16:4. Since a proper name identifies someone or something without stating its nature, the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what it names there.

word:lxx:L700744.explanation: This word means “capture”: the taking or securing of a person, place, or thing. It is a noun, so it names the result or reality of being captured rather than describing the action as a verb. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 27:46. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation and emphasis there.

word:lxx:L700810.explanation: This adjective means “carefree”: free from worry, anxiety, or troubling concern. It describes someone or something not weighed down by care. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, the word occurs twice, both in the book of Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central sense remains a condition of being untroubled or unconcerned. It is a descriptive word, not a command or action, and identifies a state marked by freedom from care.

word:lxx:L701075.explanation: This verb means “run back”: it describes moving back toward a previous place or point. As a verb, it expresses the action itself rather than a person or object. In this Greek biblical corpus, it appears only twice, both in 2 Maccabees, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The exact force—such as urgency, distance, or purpose—must be determined from each passage’s context.

word:lxx:L701097.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “brave deeds,” describing the performance of courageous actions. It presents bravery as something a person does, not merely a quality they possess. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense remains the carrying out of brave deeds.

word:lxx:L701228.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “interject” or “exchange.” It describes an action in which something is put into an exchange, especially within spoken interaction. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 11:13. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the precise force of the action in that passage must be determined from its sentence and immediate setting.

word:lxx:L701273.explanation: This verb means “speak against; answer.” It describes a spoken response that may oppose what another person has said, or may simply answer that person. Its basic function is to mark speech directed back toward someone, especially when disagreement or a reply is involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:1. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701350.explanation: Hapax means once, referring to something done or occurring a single time.

word:lxx:L701369.explanation: This noun means obstinacy: a stubborn refusal to yield or change course. It describes a settled resistance rather than a momentary hesitation, though the precise force in any sentence depends on its surrounding context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. The word therefore names a quality of persistent stubbornness, not an action or person. Its central idea is resistance that remains firm when obedience, persuasion, or correction would call for a different response.

word:lxx:L701462.explanation: This noun means “captivity; exile,” referring to the condition of people removed from their homeland and living under displacement. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, all in seven verses, with occurrences in 2 Kings and Ezra. The word therefore describes exile as a settled condition or state, rather than simply the act of leaving. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701567.explanation: Aposbennymi means to put out or extinguish.

word:lxx:L701585.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “drip”: to fall or release liquid in small drops. It describes liquid gradually coming out rather than pouring all at once. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Joel and Amos, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. As a verb, it describes the action itself; the larger significance in either passage depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

word:lxx:L701606.explanation: This noun means a “seal” or “signet”—an object or mark used to identify, authenticate, or secure something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Jeremiah and once in Ezekiel. Its central idea remains the distinguishing mark associated with a person or possession, while the surrounding verse determines its particular use. The word is rendered “seal” in both recorded occurrences.

word:lxx:L701808.explanation: This word means “bravely.” As an adverb, it describes an action carried out with courage and boldness, telling how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: the action is performed courageously rather than timidly or fearfully.

word:lxx:L701901.explanation: Asgad is a proper name, rendered “Asgad” or “Azgath.” It identifies a named individual or family designation in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including lists associated with the returned community. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific person or family connection cannot be stated more precisely. Its basic meaning is therefore the name itself: Asgad, also rendered Azgath.

word:lxx:L702038.explanation: This adjective describes something lewd—sexually improper, indecent, or morally unrestrained. It characterizes conduct or speech that violates proper sexual modesty rather than expressing a neutral description. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, the word occurs only once, in Sirach 23:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is clear: it identifies behavior or expression as lewd and improper.

word:lxx:L702063.explanation: Asor is a proper name, identifying something called “Asor” rather than expressing a general quality or action. It appears fourteen times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with most occurrences in Joshua and additional occurrences in Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 1 Maccabees. The name is rendered “Asor” in the available English support. Its specific referent in any passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

word:lxx:L702117.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person or place called “Aua” or “Ava.” It is a name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 19:13. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the individual or location named there.

word:lxx:L702391.explanation: Baithanath, also rendered “Vethanath,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX text, it identifies a named entity in Judges 1:33. The gloss gives both “Baithanath” and “Vethanath” as the name’s renderings. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, so its ordinary function is simply to identify that name; its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L702416.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Baithēra” or “Vethira.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both occurrences being in Judges 7:24. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name, not as a common noun with a broader descriptive meaning.

word:lxx:L702535.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to “Bari” or “Vari.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:36. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes its designation but does not provide further information about the person or the passage. Its precise significance there belongs to the verse’s wider context.

word:lxx:L702621.explanation: Beelmeōn is a proper name referring to a place, rendered as “Beelmeōn” or “Veelmeon.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Numbers 32:38. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific historical or contextual significance cannot be stated here; its basic function is to identify the place named Beelmeōn.

word:lxx:L702654.explanation: Berea, also called Verea, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this word appears once, in 1 Maccabees 9:4. The name itself identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, person, or spiritual concept. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s specific role in that sentence cannot be explained further. Its basic meaning is simply the place-name Berea.

word:lxx:L702733.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “sprout”: to begin growing or to spring up, especially as a plant or living growth emerges. It describes the visible beginning of growth rather than a completed mature state. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek Deuterocanonical books, including passages about plants, trees, and renewed growth. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the emergence of life and growth.

word:lxx:L702768.explanation: Bosor is a place-name. It names a city in the wilderness. It also names a brook.

word:lxx:L702786.explanation: This noun means “herd,” referring to a group of livestock or other animals kept together. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used across 20 verses, especially in passages concerning herds as part of a household’s possessions, offerings, or prosperity. Its basic sense remains concrete and collective: not one animal, but a herd viewed as a group. The word appears from Exodus through Amos in the Old Testament Greek corpus.

word:lxx:L702845.explanation: Gaam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 22:24. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who someone is called, not what that person does or represents. The name’s specific significance in Genesis 22:24 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L702900.explanation: This word is a proper name, identified as “Gai” or “Ye.” It names a person rather than describing an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 33:6. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide further details about the person or explain the surrounding verse. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the wider context of the verse and chapter.

word:lxx:L702939.explanation: This adjective means “calm,” describing someone or something marked by quietness rather than agitation or disturbance. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a peaceful or settled condition. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:6. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described further; its ordinary meaning remains a calm or tranquil state.

word:lxx:L703161.explanation: Goliath is a proper name referring to the Philistine warrior known by that name in the Greek Old Testament and in Sirach. It is not a general word describing a quality or action, but a personal designation. The name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: four times in the Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its uses refer to the same named biblical figure or to a person identified by that name, while the surrounding verse determines the particular event being mentioned.

word:lxx:L703222.explanation: Golela is a noun used as the name “Golela,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 2:13. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included, this lexical entry identifies the name but does not establish its precise referent there. That particular identification belongs to the context of the verse itself.

word:lxx:L703280.explanation: This word means “lender,” a person who provides money or other resources to someone with the expectation of repayment. As a noun, it identifies the one who gives a loan rather than the borrower who receives it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, showing a focused reference to the person involved in lending. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its teaching about debt, obligation, or repayment.

word:lxx:L703327.explanation: This Greek verb describes being “in straits” or coming to “take offense.” It can express a person’s difficult or pressured condition, or the reaction of taking offense. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central sense concerns distress or offense.

word:lxx:L703477.explanation: This noun means “attendance” or “service”—being present to help, care for, or carry out a duty. It describes an act of serving rather than a person who serves. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:58. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains practical service or attendance given to others.

word:lxx:L703543.explanation: This verb means “cross over”: to move from one side of a place or boundary to the other. It describes passage across something, whether a physical route, region, or barrier. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, with most occurrences in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being crossed and the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains movement from one side to another.

word:lxx:L703640.explanation: Diachōrizō means to divide or separate.

word:lxx:L703679.explanation: This verb means “narrate” or “describe”: to tell something in an orderly or understandable way. It can refer to recounting events, reporting what has happened, or putting an experience into words for someone else. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 64 times, showing a broad use for communicating experiences, reports, and accounts. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on what is being recounted and to whom it is told.

word:lxx:L703705.explanation: This adjective describes something made in a net-like or latticed pattern. It can refer to an object or surface formed with an open, interwoven structure rather than a solid, continuous one. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs four times, describing such construction or design. Its central idea is not a net as an object, but the quality of being “made in net fashion” or “latticed.”

word:lxx:L703802.explanation: “Dorkōn” or “Thorkon” is a proper name, identifying a person or named figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Song of Songs 2:17. The available information establishes the name itself, but not the person’s identity or significance apart from that passage. Its precise reference in the verse therefore depends on the surrounding text and context.

word:lxx:L703899.explanation: This Greek LXX proper noun is a personal name, rendered “Dōra” or “Thora.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The name occurs 73 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, across 69 verses. Its exact reference may identify different individuals, so the surrounding verse is needed to determine whom it names in a particular passage.

word:lxx:L703936.explanation: Ebrona, also rendered Evrona, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 33:34 and Numbers 33:35. The name is preserved as a name instead of being translated into an ordinary English concept. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a named designation.

word:lxx:L703983.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as “wearied”—worn down, tired, or lacking strength. It presents weariness as a condition rather than an action, helping identify the state of the person or thing described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Job, Ecclesiastes, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central meaning remains a state of weariness or exhaustion.

word:lxx:L704047.explanation: Ezer is a personal name, preserved as a name rather than translated into a descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in 1 Chronicles 7:21 and once in Ezekiel 11:1. Because the available information identifies it only as Ezer, its central meaning is the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person bears it in each passage.

word:lxx:L704182.explanation: “From there” is an adverb that points back to a place, direction, or location already understood in the sentence or surrounding passage. It tells where someone or something comes from or the point from which movement or action proceeds. This word occurs 134 times in the Greek Septuagint corpus, including passages from Genesis through later deuterocanonical writings. Its exact reference—what place “there” identifies—comes from the surrounding context of each verse.

word:lxx:L704201.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “clean out”—to remove what is present so that something is cleared. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in Deuteronomy and once in Judges. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the deliberate removal or clearing out of something.

word:lxx:L704274.explanation: Ekpempō means to send out or dispatch.

word:lxx:L704308.explanation: This verb means to have the flesh stripped off—that is, to describe flesh being removed from something. It is a physical action word, not a general term for harm or injury. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 24:4; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular force there. Its wording focuses on the removal of flesh, presenting the condition or result rather than naming the person who performs the action.

word:lxx:L704353.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “cancel; set aside.” It describes an action that removes something from effect or places it to one side rather than allowing it to stand or continue. As a verb, it expresses what someone does, not a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 7:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is to cancel something or set it aside.

word:lxx:L704432.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to an “elephant” or to “ivory,” naming either the animal itself or the valuable material associated with it. Its exact sense is determined by how the sentence uses the word. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 6:46. No broader usage pattern is available from additional occurrences, so the central meaning remains the straightforward identification of an elephant or ivory.

word:lxx:L704490.explanation: Elisous, also rendered Elisus, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 5:15. The available wording provides the name itself but does not establish an additional lexical meaning or explain the person’s role. Its significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, not on a broader abstract definition of the name.

word:lxx:L704524.explanation: This LXX noun means “such and such,” referring to a person or thing that is left unnamed or identified only generally. It functions as a substitute designation rather than giving the person’s or thing’s specific name. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 6:8. Its basic sense is therefore brief and indefinite: it points to someone or something understood in the situation without naming it directly.

word:lxx:L704551.explanation: Emblepō means to look at. It can also mean to look in.

word:lxx:L704726.explanation: This noun means a “pledge” or “surety”—something given as a guarantee for an obligation or promise. It describes security connected with a debt or responsibility, rather than the debt itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Deuteronomy 24:10–13. Its precise force in any individual sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is a pledged guarantee or security.

word:lxx:L704793.explanation: Enteuthen means from here. It can also mean from this or that side.

word:lxx:L704850.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “leap out of” or “leap up.” It describes a sudden jumping movement away from a place or upward from it. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nahum 3:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from that context; but its basic action is a quick, energetic leap or springing movement.

word:lxx:L704928.explanation: This LXX verb means “sound out”: to make something heard or announce it aloud. It describes the act of giving a sound public expression rather than keeping it silent. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Joel, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains vocalizing or broadcasting something so that it can be heard.

word:lxx:L704973.explanation: This verb means to disdain someone or something—to treat it as unworthy of regard or to set it at naught. It expresses rejection, contempt, or the refusal to value what is before you. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: regarding someone or something with contempt rather than honor or esteem.

word:lxx:L705035.explanation: This noun means an “enchanter” or “charmer”: a person associated with enchantment or the use of charms. It appears 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. The word serves as a label for such practitioners, rather than describing an ordinary skill or occupation. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L705116.explanation: This adjective means “towards the right,” describing a direction or position on the right side. It identifies where something is oriented or located rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:16. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains directional: movement or orientation toward the right. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

word:lxx:L705268.explanation: Epistēmōn means an expert, someone possessing knowledge and skill.

word:lxx:L705286.explanation: This verb describes something dangerous or risky—something that may lead to harm, loss, or an uncertain outcome. It expresses the quality of being unsafe rather than naming a particular danger. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Wisdom 9:14. Its basic sense remains concise: what is dangerous or risky requires caution and cannot be treated as secure.

word:lxx:L705321.explanation: This verb means “shine on”: it describes light giving brightness or falling upon something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job, so its basic sense is focused rather than broad or varied. The word may be used for light that visibly shines, while the surrounding verse determines what is being illuminated. Its central idea remains the active presence or effect of shining. citep03:word:lxx:L705321:identity citep03:word:lxx:L705321:occurrences

word:lxx:L705354.explanation: This verb means to “stir up” or “excite,” describing an action that awakens, encourages, or intensifies a response. It focuses on moving someone or something toward stronger activity or feeling rather than simply naming a state. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the deliberate stirring or rousing of a response.

word:lxx:L705563.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that is well-known or familiar. It points to what is recognized and known rather than unknown or obscure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Proverbs, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the surrounding verse determines exactly what person or thing is being described. The word appears in Proverbs 3:15, 5:6, and 33:26.

word:lxx:L705772.explanation: Ephod is the name of an ephod, a noun referring to a particular biblical item. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears four times, all in Judges, from Judges 17:5 through Judges 18:20. Its lexical meaning is simply “ephod,” without a fuller description of the item’s purpose or significance. That specific force must be understood from the surrounding passage in each verse.

word:lxx:L705804.explanation: Zabdias is a proper name, also rendered Zavthias. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears three times, in three verses: once in 1 Chronicles and twice in 2 Chronicles. The name itself does not provide further meaning about the individuals who bear it; their identity and role must be understood from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L705871.explanation: Zēlos means zeal. It can also mean jealousy.

word:lxx:L705952.explanation: Ētham, also rendered Itham, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word with a translated meaning. It identifies a named figure or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek Psalms, at Psalm 73:15. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

word:lxx:L706052.explanation: Thaanach is a proper name, also given as “Thaanakh.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 4:12 and 1 Chronicles 7:29. Those references establish where the name appears, while the name’s precise referent in each passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L706104.explanation: Thara is a proper name used as a personal designation, not a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the name is rendered simply “Thara.” It occurs 11 times across 9 verses, chiefly in Genesis, with additional occurrences in Joshua and 1 Chronicles. The listed Genesis occurrences span Genesis 11:24–31, showing that the name belongs to the genealogical and family-history material found there. Its meaning is therefore its identity as the name Thara, rather than an abstract quality or ordinary vocabulary term.

word:lxx:L706171.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to a person’s will or desire—the intention, preference, or purpose someone has. It can describe what a person wants or chooses, and its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Daniel, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its central idea remains the inward desire or decision that directs a person’s action.

word:lxx:L706276.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means pressure. It describes a condition in which someone is pressed, constrained, or placed under difficult force. The word occurs 129 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring term for hardship or oppressive circumstances rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L706298.explanation: This adjective describes someone who is bold of heart—innerly confident, daring, or self-assured rather than timid. It points to a person’s inward disposition, especially the courage or boldness expressed through the heart.
